intro: Kenya is one of the places where humanity began, a land of Swahili trading towns, and a nation that fought for its freedom from Britain.

chapters.title: Cradle of humankind
text: Fossils from around Lake Turkana include 'Turkana Boy', a nearly complete skeleton of an early human about 1.5 million years old. Stone tools found there are some of the oldest known.
Later, Bantu-speaking farmers, Nilotic herders like the Maasai, and Cushitic peoples settled the region.

chapters.title: Swahili coast
text: From around 800, towns like Lamu, Malindi and Mombasa traded with Arabia, Persia, India and China. Swahili culture and language grew from African and Arab influences.
Portugal built Fort Jesus in Mombasa in 1593; Oman later took control of the coast.

chapters.title: British rule and Mau Mau
text: Britain made Kenya a protectorate in 1895 and built a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria. White settlers took the best farmland in the highlands.
In the 1950s the Mau Mau uprising fought British rule; tens of thousands of Kenyans were detained in camps, and many were killed. Kenya became independent in 1963, led by Jomo Kenyatta.

highlight.title: Mau Mau
highlight.text: In 2013 Britain paid compensation to Kenyans tortured during the uprising.

chapters.title: Since independence
text: Kenya became a one-party state, then returned to multi-party politics in 1991. Violence after the 2007 election killed over 1,000 people. A new constitution in 2010 shared power with 47 counties. In 2024 young people led protests against tax rises.

timeline.title: Turkana Boy
timeline.text: An early human lives by the lake.

keyTerms.meaning: A coastal culture and a language spoken across East Africa.
